extracted.intended_audience: general public interested in humor research, psychologists, comedians and writers
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the LaughLab crowd-sourced experiment that collected jokes and had people rate randomly selected jokes, reporting findings about what kinds of jokes scored highly. Useful as a guide to empirical measurement of joke funniness and factors that influence perceived humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-point funniness rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rated how funny they found five randomly selected jokes on a five-point scale ranging from ‘not very funny’ to ‘very funny’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each rater evaluated five jokes chosen at random; using a simple ordinal 1–5 funniness scale enabled aggregation across large numbers of raters. This is the primary quantitative measure used to identify 'top' jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect basic demographic information
rubrics_metrics.description: People could answer a few simple questions about themselves (such as their sex, age, and nationality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demographics were recorded to allow analysis of differences in joke ratings by sex, age, and nationality (e.g., the top American joke differed from the overall top joke). Collecting these fields enables subgroup comparisons and cultural analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean-content archival filter
rubrics_metrics.description: LaughLab provides downloads of jokes and notes that over 1,000 of the LaughLab jokes are 'all clean!'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project maintained a clean-joke subset for distribution; when producing or evaluating jokes for mass/public archives, consider explicit content filters and produce a labeled 'clean' set if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to media seeding and priming
rubrics_metrics.description: External media attention (Dave Barry's column) caused the site to receive large numbers of the same punchline ('There’s a weasel chomping on my privates') and influenced which jokes rose to prominence (the top American joke was weasel-oriented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that publicity or suggestions can flood an experiment with seeded variants and bias results. When evaluating crowd-sourced humor data, check for and account for meme-driven submission spikes and priming effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic/phonological effects (the 'comedy k')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'k' sound (as in the 'hard c') is associated with words like 'Quack' and 'duck' and 'has long been seen by comedians and comedy writers as being especially funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The team re-entered a simple animal/noise joke with different animals and noises; the duck/quack variant placed first, which supports the idea that specific phonetic sounds (the 'k' sound) can increase perceived funniness. Consider phonetic shape when crafting or evaluating jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection and surprise punchline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the Sherlock Holmes/Watson tent joke and the two-hunters emergency-call joke use a set-up followed by a twist (surprise) punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes often rely on setup leading the audience to one inference and then delivering an unexpected reinterpretation (the punchline). Timing and concise framing (short setup, sharp twist) appear important based on the winning examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-authored vs. computer-generated quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of jokes produced by a computer programme received some of the lowest ratings in the archive, though a few (e.g., 'What kind of murderer has fibre? A cereal killer.') performed surprisingly well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-generated jokes tended to rate poorly overall; exceptions occur when simple puns or wordplay align with human expectations. When evaluating algorithmic humor, compare against human baselines and expect many failures but occasional strong simple puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to coordinated or repetitive submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: After Dave Barry's column urged readers to submit 'weasel chomping' jokes, the website received over 1,500 such submissions in a few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd-sourced joke collections can be swamped by repetitive or coordinated submissions following publicity or outside prompts. For fair evaluation, detect and mitigate large numbers of near-duplicate entries and consider deduplication or weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/therapeutic function of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner's submitter (a psychiatrist) noted that the joke 'makes people feel better, because it reminds them that there is always someone out there who is doing something more stupid than themselves'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One evaluative dimension is the psychological effect on listeners (e.g., relief, schadenfreude, reassurance). Jokes that produce a relatable comparative boost may be judged positively for social or therapeutic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and cross-cultural sampling as methodological standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The project collected 40,000 jokes rated by more than 350,000 people from 70 countries and used these large numbers to identify top jokes and patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, diverse samples enable analysis of cross-cultural differences and more robust identification of patterns. When empirically evaluating humor, aim for broad sampling across countries and many raters to detect reliable effects.
